AbstractText.Label: STUDY QUESTION
AbstractText.content: Is there an association between polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and the sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) rs1799941, rs6257, rs6259 and rs727428 variants in a large series of Mediterranean women?

AbstractText.Label: SUMMARY ANSWER
AbstractText.content: The rs727428 and rs6259 variants are associated with PCOS in Mediterranean women.

AbstractText.Label: WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY
AbstractText.content: The level of SHBG, the primary plasma transport protein for sex steroids, which regulates the bioavailability of these hormones to target tissues, is reduced in patients with PCOS. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms in the SHBG gene influence circulating SHBG levels in American patients with PCOS and may predict the development of type 2 diabetes.

AbstractText.Label: STUDY DESIGN, SIZE AND DURATION
AbstractText.content: This was a genetic case-control association study including 1004 premenopausal Mediterranean women.

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING AND METHODS
AbstractText.content: In an Academic setting, we genotyped a clinical cohort consisting of 281 patients with PCOS and 142 women without any evidence of androgen excess, and a population-based cohort comprised of 581 unselected female blood donors from Spain and Italy. The latter included 31 patients with PCOS and 550 controls, of whom 298 had no evidence of any androgen excess disorder and were considered hyper-normal controls.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE
AbstractText.content: Mutant alleles of the rs727428 variant were more frequent in patients with PCOS compared with controls and with hyper-normal controls. This association was independent of obesity. Carrying mutant alleles of rs727428 was found to be associated with a 1.29 odds ratio (OR) for PCOS, whereas carrying mutant alleles of rs6259 associated with a 0.68 OR for PCOS. The rs1799941 and rs6257 variants were not associated with PCOS. None of the SHBG variants influenced serum SHBG concentrations.

AbstractText.Label: LIMITATIONS AND REASONS FOR CAUTION
AbstractText.content: The associations found here were relatively weak and, arising from a case-control study, do not necessarily indicate a causative role of the SHBG variants in the development of PCOS. Also, we studied different patients and controls from different sources, making some of the interpretations difficult. Finally, the rs1799941 variant was not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in the small group of patients with PCOS recruited from the general population, yet this variant was not associated with PCOS.

AbstractText.Label: WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS
AbstractText.content: SHBG variants that influenced circulating SHBG levels in American patients with PCOS are also associated with this syndrome in Mediterranean women, pointing to SHBG as a candidate gene for PCOS.
